title: At the shop
goal: Shop for groceries, and set up the third case: the genitive — the form for possession, the form for "of" and "from", and the form you've been using quietly since unit 5.
bekal: put nouns into the genitive after *do, z, od, bez* and after measures
show possession without a word like "'s"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nákup na večeru
dialogs.intro: Budi is shopping to cook dinner. Eva comes along and gives advice in the aisles.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: What do you need for the soup?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kilo zemiakov, dve cibule a kúsok mäsa.

lines.text: A niečo na pitie? Máš doma vodu?

notes: **Kilo zemiakov, fľaša vody, liter mlieka, kúsok mäsa** — every measure is followed by the genitive. This is the genitive job you'll need most in daily life, and it already appeared in unit 4 (*pohár vody*) without explanation. Now the pattern is complete.

**Bez chleba, bez cukru** — the preposition *bez* always takes the genitive. Notice two different endings for two masculine words: *chlieb → chleba* takes *-a*, *cukor → cukru* takes *-u*. Both are right for their own word, and the choice has to be learned word by word.

**Do polievky** — the preposition *do* also takes the genitive. It means "into" for direction (*do školy*, *do obchodu*) and "for" when talking about ingredients (*do polievky* = to go into the soup).
**Nemám nič** — a double negative again. *Nič* on its own already means "nothing", and the verb must still be negated.

**Pre teba** takes the accusative, not the genitive. The preposition *pre* (for) is one of the few that demand the accusative — along with *na* and *cez* when they express direction or purpose. Don't confuse it with *bez* and *do*, which sit right next to it in the same sentence.

grammars.title: The genitive — the third case, and the busiest
body: The genitive answers *koho?* (of whom) and *čoho?* (of what). It has five different jobs, and you've already used three of them without noticing.
after: **The adjective**: m and n take **-ého** (*bez dobrého chleba*), f takes **-ej** (*do novej školy*). Two more endings, just like the locative.

**Rows two and three are the only ones that need learning word by word.** The tendency: solid things you can hold and count take *-a* (*chleba, syra, stola*), while places, shapeless materials, and abstract things take *-u* (*obchodu, cukru, času*). The tendency leaks in many places, so note the ending down with the word.

**The five jobs of the genitive**, all already seen in this course: (1) after numbers 5 and up — unit 5; (2) after measures — *kilo, fľaša, pohár, kúsok*; (3) possession — *kniha brata*; (4) after the prepositions *do, z, od, bez, okrem, počas*; (5) after *veľa, málo, koľko*.

grammars.title: Possession without "'s"
body: Slovak shows possession by putting **the owner** into the genitive and placing it **after** the thing owned. No linking word at all.
after: **The order is the one English uses with "of"**: the thing first, the owner after — "the book of the brother", never "the brother's book". *Kniha brata* follows exactly that order; all Slovak adds is the ending.
**For an owner you'd name with a pronoun, the possessive is more natural**: *moja kniha* (my book), not *kniha mňa*. The genitive is used when the owner is a noun, not a pronoun.

**People's names change too**: *auto Evy* (Eva's car), *kniha Budiho* (Budi's book). Foreign male names usually get *-a* or *-ho*, female names ending in *-a* get *-y*. Slovaks do this to foreign names without hesitation — don't be surprised when your own name changes shape.

blocks.title: Words with a story
items: *Ryža* and *cesnak* may sound strange, but *paradajka* (tomato) has a story: it comes from *paradajské jablko*, "apple of paradise". Just like Hungarian *paradicsom*.
*Kuracie mäso* = chicken meat. To order chicken in a restaurant, that's the form you need, not *kura*.
*Bravčové* = pork, *hovädzie* = beef, *kuracie* = chicken. All three are adjectives, and you need to recognize all three if you avoid certain meats.
To state a dietary rule: *Nejem bravčové mäso* (I don't eat pork) or *Jem len halal* (I only eat halal). Bratislava has a few halal restaurants; in small towns, ask with the first sentence.

blocks.text: Every word in the left column is followed by the genitive. Learn the pairs whole, and the genitive will feel natural within a week.

Look at **deko**: in Slovakia and the Czech Republic, cheese and cold cuts are sold in *deka* (decagrams, 10 grams each). *Dvadsať deka* means 200 grams. It's confusing until you've heard it twice; after that it's natural.

head: Phrases in the shop
English
rows: I'd like half a kilo of cheese.
I'll pay by card / in cash.

blocks.text: **Do for going in, z for coming out.** These two always work together: *do školy* / *zo školy*, *do obchodu* / *z obchodu*, *do Bratislavy* / *z Bratislavy*. Learn one and you get the other for free.

**Od for people, z for places.** *Idem od lekára* (I'm coming from the doctor — the person), *idem z nemocnice* (I'm coming from the hospital — the building). The distinction is subtle and beginners often ignore it; getting it right sounds very polished.
